title: Multiway pots
summary: Three or more players after the flop: fewer bluffs, stronger value, the nut draws gain.

why.text: A **multiway** pot has three or more players after the flop. Every extra opponent is one more range that may have hit. Against two players the chance that someone has a pair or better is roughly twice as high as against one.

changes.text:
What changes:
- **Fewer bluffs**: to win the pot everyone has to fold. If each folds 50% of the time, both fold together only 25%.
- **Stronger value**: top pair with a weak kicker against three players is more often a check.
- **Fewer c-bets**, mostly with strong hands and strong draws.
- **Nut draws** gain value: the ace-high flush draw wins big pots, a smaller flush can lose to a bigger one.

mdf.text: In a multiway pot MDF is shared: if someone bets pot into two players, together you need to defend about 50%, not 50% each. Each player can continue less often, especially the one who acts first.

q-fold.q: You bluff into two opponents, each folds 60% of the time. How often do both fold?
q-fold.explain: 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36: the bluff works only about a third of the time.

t1.q: Why bluff less in multiway pots?
t1.explain: Fold chances multiply and drop fast.

t2.q: Which draws are especially valuable multiway?
t2.explain: When they hit they win, and multiway pots get big.

t3.q: Top pair with a weak kicker against three opponents is usually…
options: A hand for three streets of value
t3.explain: Someone often has a better kicker or two pair.
